etymologies.etymologyHTML:
Inherited from Middle English rubben, of unknown origin; possibly ultimately from Proto-Germanic *rubbōną, related to *reufaną (“to tear”).

Cognate with Saterland Frisian rubje (“to rub, scrape”), German Low German rubben (“to rub”), Low German rubblig (“rough, uneven”), Dutch robben, rubben (“to rub smooth; scrape; scrub”), Danish rubbe (“to rub, scrub”), Icelandic and Norwegian rubba (“to scrape”). More at reave.

quote.citation: c. 1599–1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Hamlet, Prince of Denmarke”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene i]:
quote.text: To die, to sleep— / To sleep—perchance to dream. Ay, there's the rub! / For in that sleep of death what dreams may come, / When we have shuffled off this mortal coil, / Must give us pause

quote.citation: 1922 February, James Joyce, “[[Episode 16]]”, in Ulysses, Paris: Shakespeare and Company, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: […]  the propriety of the cabman's shelter, as it was called, hardly a stonesthrow away near Butt bridge where they might hit upon some drinkables in the shape of a milk and soda or a mineral. But how to get there was the rub.

quote.citation: 1863, Sheridan Le Fanu, The House by the Churchyard:
quote.text: 'My dear Devereux, I say, you mustn't talk in that wild way. You—you talk like a ruined man!''And I so comfortable!''Why, to be sure, Dick, you have had some little rubs, and, maybe, your follies and your vexations; but, hang it, you are young; you can't get experience—at least, so I've found it—without paying for it.  […] '

definitions.definition: In the game of crown green bowls, any obstacle by which a bowl is diverted from its normal course.
A mixture of spices applied to meat before it is barbecued.
Any substance designed to be applied by rubbing.
(transitive) To move (one object) while maintaining contact with another object over some area, with pressure and friction.

quote.citation: 1680, T. K., The Kitchin-Phyſician; Or, a Guide for Good-Housewives in Maintaining Their Families in Health.  […] ‎[1], How to cleanſe the Teeth, and keep them ſound, page 44:
quote.text: You ſhould rub your Teeth and whole Mouth and Gums, the Pallate and Tongue, with a clean courſe cloth, rubbing off the ſlime which groweth upon them in the night.

quote.citation: 1918, W[illiam] B[abington] Maxwell, chapter VII, in The Mirror and the Lamp, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: […]  Walden rubbed his hands together and smiled contentedly.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To spread a substance thinly over; to smear.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book I”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: The smoothed plank,  […]  / New rubbed with balm.

definitions.definition: (dated) To move or pass with difficulty.
To scour; to burnish; to polish; to brighten; to cleanse; often with up or over.

quote.citation: a. 1716, Robert South, Man Created in God's Image:
quote.text: The whole business of our redemption is, in short, only to rub over the defaced copy of the creation

definitions.definition: To hinder; to cross; to thwart.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1606, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of King Lear”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene ii]:
quote.text: 'Tis the duke's pleasure, / Whose disposition, all the world well knows, / Will not be rubbed nor stopped.

definitions.definition: (transitive, bowls) To touch the jack with the bowl.
